snippet.title: Grand Larceny Longplay (Commodore 64 Game)
snippet.description:
- Grand Larceny Longplay (Commodore 64 Game) -

Grand Larceny is an action-adventure developed by Beam Software and published by Melbourne House for the Commodore 64 in 1984. It combines side-view exploration with text-adventure mechanics, placing the player inside the Grand Hotel with one clear assignment: infiltrate the building, steal the plans for a new supercomputer and escape from the roof by helicopter before midnight.

The interface is unusual for its time. The upper half of the screen shows the protagonist walking through horizontally scrolling locations, controlled directly with the joystick, while more complex actions are entered through a text parser below. Only a small vocabulary is recognized, with around two dozen verbs covering actions such as opening doors, searching objects, giving items and interacting with the people encountered inside the hotel.

Progress is built around fairly traditional adventure-game logic. Useful objects are hidden around the building, certain characters must be approached in the correct way, and several obstacles require a specific command or item before the route forward becomes available. One memorable sequence involves finding flowers for a secretary before reaching the safe containing the plans, after which the player still has to work out how to reach the eventual escape route.

For such an early hybrid, the combination of direct movement and typed interaction is interesting. Walking around makes the world feel more physical than a conventional text adventure, while the command system allows situations to be slightly more elaborate than a straightforward arcade game could manage. The animated results of successful actions also give puzzles a little more personality.

Unfortunately, the pacing is where the whole thing starts to unravel.

Time passes continuously, and the final route to the roof does not become available until 11:00. That sounds atmospheric on paper: steal the plans, evade the hotel staff and wait for the right moment to escape before midnight. In practice, if you know what you are doing, the adventure can be solved far too early.

That is exactly what happened during my playthrough. I reached the point where there was effectively nothing useful left to do at around 8:28, yet the roof remained inaccessible until much later. The result was more than twenty minutes of simply killing time in a video lasting only a little over half an hour.

There are technically things the player can do while waiting — wander around the hotel, search for optional objects, visit the bar or explore rooms that are no longer necessary — but none of that changes the fundamental problem. Once the required puzzles have been solved, the game is deliberately preventing progress until its internal clock catches up.

It is a strange design choice because it punishes efficiency. Adventure games normally reward the player for understanding their puzzles; here, solving them quickly can leave you with the least interesting part of the experience by far. The real-time deadline creates tension when you are still trying to work things out, but once the solution is known, that same system becomes dead weight.

Movement does not help much either. The walking speed can be adjusted, which is useful because the slower settings are almost painfully sluggish, but even at maximum speed the repeated trips through the hotel can feel drawn out. The scrolling graphics are functional rather than attractive, though the changing music does give the otherwise sparse presentation some atmosphere.

The puzzles themselves are not especially deep, but there is a certain charm in the mixture of espionage, hotel exploration and slightly absurd interactions. At its best, the game feels like a primitive predecessor to later graphic adventures: move a character around a visible world, type an action, watch the result and gradually piece together the correct sequence.

The problem is that the final wait overwhelms much of that goodwill. A 31-minute successful run containing roughly 22 minutes where virtually nothing needs to happen is difficult to defend as good pacing.

So the old description still says it best: don't be fooled by the length. There is a lot of time to kill here. Grand Larceny has an interesting hybrid structure and some enjoyable ideas, but once the mystery has been solved, the clock becomes its greatest enemy.

#retrogamingloft #grandlarceny #commodore64
